title: Chapter 152 – Who Keeps the Garden
html:
[Lin Garden – Tian Mo]

Tian Mo has stood on the same step of the Gate stair for twenty-three years, and the first thing he learns on the morning the Keeper leaves is that a man can stand in one place and still be moved.

It is a cold clear dawn, the second week of the new year. The frost on the seven hundred and one steps is white and unbroken, and the blue lamps in the niches burn low. He is at the fifth landing, where he always is, with his staff planted and his knees bent and his weight resting evenly on the balls of his feet. Below him the Dock is silent. The Gate wall is a plain black wall. Three weeks ago it was something else, and the memory of that brightness still sits behind his eyes like the afterimage of a lamp.

He is thirty-four. He is tall and spare, with the heavy shoulders of a man who has done one thing with great patience for a very long time, and a scar through his left eyebrow that he got at the age of twelve when he fell off a wall. He has never spoken much. He sometimes thinks it is because the first person who ever taught him anything said so little.

Stand, Kuang said. That was the whole of the lesson. They have to come through you.

He does not move. But he is aware, as the light comes down the stair, that the words have stopped sounding like an instruction and begun to sound like a question.

"Master Tian."

It is a small voice from above. He looks up. Bell stands at the head of the landing with a satchel over one shoulder and a blanket over the other, in the plain blue gown of the Garden clinic. She is thirty-seven and has been correcting her elders since she could walk. Her face this morning is scrubbed and very serious.

"The Keeper is calling a council," she says. "In the long hall. At the second bell. He asked that you come."

"I hold the stair."

"He said you would say that." Bell almost smiles. "He said to tell you that this is about the stair."

* * *

The long hall of the Lin Garden has been rebuilt four times, and every time it has come out a little larger.

It is a low timber building with a high pitched roof, a hundred feet from end to end, and on a winter morning with the stoves lit it smells of smoke and wet wool and tea. The long trestle table down the middle has been swept clean. On it lie a ledger, a roll of maps, three cups, and a small gray stone creature with a white line down his back, who sits at the head of the table like a clerk.

They are all there. Tian Mo counts them as he comes in, from habit. Head Han, in her plain gray robe, rigid as a sword, with the jade seal on a cord at her neck. Lu Fei beside her, with her roll under her arm. Old Pei An, seventy-nine, with a stick and a thin cheerful face. Lan Wen, tall and gray, with his white eyes lifted to the beams. Ning Ruiyan, broad and scarred, in a smock stained with ink. Feng, in a heavy wool blanket, with his head tilted. Zhao and her husband, and Yue, with her hands in her lap, and at the end of the table, in a plain brown cloak, with his white hair tied back and a cup of tea steaming before him, the Keeper.

And at the foot, in the chair that nobody else would dare to sit in, small and straight in her blue smock, Qinghe, with her arms folded.

"Sit, Tian," she says. "You look like you have swallowed a rake."

He sits. Jian waits until the room settles. When he speaks, his voice is mild and dry and carries without effort.

"I am leaving in nine days."

No one is surprised. It has been known since the night of the message. But hearing it in that plain voice seems to change the air in the room, as if a window has been opened. Zhao draws a breath. Lu Fei's knuckles whiten on the roll.

"The road Ning has found is a line of light from the ring of stars to the old house," says Jian. "It is fading. By his count it will last forty days. Pebble says the sixth door cannot be reached unless we are on that road. I have no wish to hurry, but I have no wish to miss it either." He turns his cup. "I want to tell you what I plan to leave, and what I need. And I want you to tell me where I am wrong."

* * *

He lays it out in order, as he does everything.

The Seat. The Lin Seat, granted in the year of the Chain, has a ruling Keeper and a council of nine. With the Keeper away it needs a regent. He proposes Head Han, who holds the Sect's seal and whose Court has held Article Forty-four for twenty-three years. Han says nothing for a moment. Then she inclines her head, with the air of a woman accepting a debt she has long expected.

"I accept," she says. "On one condition."

"Name it."

"That you do not stay away so long that I become fond of the work."

There is a faint laugh. It dies quickly.

The Roll. The Roll of the Keepers is a living thing, written on the Gate wall, and it will not close in his absence. Someone must read it. Jian proposes Pei An. The old man looks up, startled, and a little frightened, and then, slowly, very slightly, he smiles.

"I have burned eleven names," he says. "I would be honored to keep a thousand."

"You will have help." Jian nods to Lan Wen, who has not moved. "He will read the Hollow ledger. The rest of the Order's archive is in the Registry hall. You two know it better than anyone alive."

"We will manage," says Lan Wen, in his flat quiet voice. "We have both been ledgers. It's a hard habit to break."

The Garden. Jian looks down the table, and for a moment his eyes rest on his mother. "The clan stands at eleven hundred and four. It is the largest it has ever been. It will need a head who can say no to the Sect, to the Treasury and to its own relations." A faint, wry curve of the lips. "I propose Zhao."

Zhao flushes to the roots of her hair. "Uncle—"

"You counted every cart in the winter of the siege. You fed seven hundred strangers. You named your son for a man you never met, and you held a ledger without being asked." He shrugs. "I do not know a better definition of a head of clan."

"I have three children."

"So did I, at your age. In a manner of speaking." He smiles. "You will manage."

Zhao looks at her husband. He is a quiet young man of the Court, in neat gray, with a stubborn jaw. He puts a hand on her shoulder and says nothing at all, and it appears to be enough.

"And the stair," says Jian.

He does not look at Tian Mo. He does not need to. Tian feels the whole room turn.

* * *

"I am not asking you to take the Dock," Jian says. "I am asking you to stand on it."

Tian Mo sits very still. His hands are flat on his knees.

"The Gate is closed. The Dock is dark. I do not think anything will come out of it. But there is a thing on the other side of that wall that has been waiting a long time for a door, and the road I take will not close it. It will only turn the lamp on." He sets down his cup. "I am leaving a Garden of eleven hundred and a Sect of nine thousand and a hundred and fifty years of paper. I cannot protect them. What I can do is leave them a man who knows how to stand."

"The Warden of the Stair," says Han, quietly. "It is an old title. It has not been used since the Founders."

"It is a good one."

Tian Mo finds that he cannot speak. The words are there. They rise behind his teeth, a dry hard knot. He thinks of a mountain. He thinks of a boy of eleven with a blanket around his neck and a staff too tall for him. He thinks: I did not need to stand. He had said it, in the golden light, to a heap of dust, and been ashamed. It had not been true. He had needed to stand more than he had ever needed anything.

"I would be glad," he says. His voice comes out cracked. "To keep it."

"Thank you."

"For how long?"

Jian hesitates. It is a very small hesitation, and Tian Mo, who has spent twenty-three years watching the shape of silence, sees it.

"I do not know," says the Keeper. "That is the truth. If the road is kind, a year. If not..."

"If not?"

"Then longer."

The room is very quiet. Beside the table, on the bench, Pebble shifts. The white line on his spine glows faintly in the lamp-light.

It will not be kind, he says, in his deep slow voice, to no one in particular. It was not made to be.

* * *

The council breaks for tea. Tian Mo does not drink his.

He walks out onto the porch of the long hall and stands in the cold with his hands behind his back and looks down the slope to the orchard. The trees are black and bare. The snow lies in patches. It is bright and clean and extremely still, and a long way off, on the shoulder of Cloud Peak, he can see the dome of the observatory catching the first sun.

"You are brooding," says a voice behind him.

"I am thinking."

"It looks the same." Feng limps up beside him, wrapped in his blanket, and leans on the rail. He is ninety, thin as a reed, with gray hair and a sharp, humorous, unfocused face, and he smells of liniment. "I used to stand like that, you know. When I was your age. I thought it made me look wise."

"Did it?"

"It made me look constipated." Feng coughs, and laughs, and the laugh turns into a cough again. "I'm sorry. I am not here to be funny. I am here because I heard you."

Tian Mo says nothing.

"Not the words. The seam in your chest." Feng's head tilts. "You are afraid. It is a very small note. Like a bird that thinks it has seen a cat."

"I'm not afraid of the stair."

"No. Of course not." The old man's voice is kind. "It is the other thing. You think you are not the right man. You think Kuang would have been better. You think, he stood for forty years and I have stood for twenty and I have not even killed anyone." He pauses. "Am I close?"

Tian Mo is silent for a long time. The wind stirs the bare branches. A crow lifts off the orchard wall and wheels, once, and settles.

"Yes," he says.

"Good." Feng reaches over and pats his arm. "That is how I know you are the right one. Kuang was afraid for forty years. He just never said so."

* * *

In the afternoon he goes to the observatory with Ning Ruiyan.

It is an hour's climb, and neither of them speaks. The big man leads, with his roll of paper under his arm and his scarred face turned always a little toward the sky. At the top the dome stands against a blue so deep it is almost black, and the door is open, and inside the vast spiral chart climbs the wall in blue ink and white chalk, as bright as the day it was drawn.

"I wanted you to see it," says Ning.

"Why me?"

"Because you will keep the gate when we are gone." He sets down the roll. "Look."

He points. In the upper curve of the wall, in red ink, the ring of eleven stars burns on its page, and from the gap at its center a thin straight line of silver has been drawn all the way down the dome to the floor, where it ends in a small neat circle. The circle is labelled in his careful hand: The old house.

"That is the road," says Ning. "Forty days. It narrows a little every night. I have measured it with a string." He swallows. "But that is not what I wanted to show you."

He leads him around the wall to the north side, where the chart thins and the paper is yellow and brittle. There, at the edge of the known sky, below the Weaver's Girl and the Southern Fish, he has drawn a long jagged line in black.

"The Sky Wall," says Ning. "The mountains at the end of the world. Nine years ago, when I began this, I drew the peaks. They were fixed. They are not fixed now." He taps the line with a thick finger. "Last winter the second peak shifted two fingers east. This winter it has shifted another four. Lu Fei has been taking Weights readings from the southern tower. Something very large is moving behind the Wall."

"Beasts?"

"Perhaps." The scar wrinkles. "I do not know. But the movement began on the night the Archivist died. And it has not stopped."

Tian Mo looks at the black line. He does not say anything. But a cold, quiet, definite thing settles in his chest, like a stone dropped into a well, and he knows it is the sound of his own name being called.

They have to come through you.

"Tell the Keeper," he says.

"I did. He said to tell you."

"Why?"

"Because he is leaving," says Ning gently, "and you are staying."

* * *

On the sixth day, Zhao hears her first petitioners.

It is not an official occasion. She has no seat, no robe, no hall. She simply sits at the end of the trestle table in the long hall at noon, with her ledger open and a cup of tea at her elbow, and by the second bell there is a line of fourteen people out the door. Tian Mo, passing on his way to the stair, stops in the doorway without meaning to.

A farmer wants to know whether the new families from the Orchard villages may plant on the north slope. An old woman complains that the school is too noisy. Two cousins have quarreled over a plow. A young mother, red-eyed and shy, says that her husband has been taken by the Sect's levy, and asks, in a whisper, if the clan might speak for him. Zhao listens to each. She does not interrupt. She writes it down, in her small clear hand, and when the last has finished she looks up with her mother's tilted head and says, in a steady voice, "I will answer all of them by tomorrow. The plow today."

The cousins stare. She calls them forward and settles it in four sentences. They go out looking vaguely ashamed and strangely pleased.

"You are doing very well," says Tian Mo, from the door.

"I am terrified." Zhao does not look up. She is writing. "My hands have been shaking since sunrise. I keep thinking, someone will notice, and send for Grandmother."

"Grandmother is cooking."

"Yes. Thank goodness." She sets down the brush at last and rubs her eyes. She looks tired, and rather young, and entirely like herself. "Master Tian. May I ask you something?"

"Yes."

"Is it always like this? Holding a thing?"

He considers. He thinks of the cold stair, the long nights, the weight of the staff.

"Yes," he says. "And you stop noticing. And then one day somebody asks you, and you cannot remember when it stopped being heavy."

She smiles, a small crooked pleased smile.

"That is not a comfort," she says.

"No. It is the truth."

* * *

Bell finds him in the storeroom on the seventh day, up to her elbows in jars.

It is the clinic's reserve, a long cold room under the old house with rows of shelves, and she is working through it with the ferocity of a woman packing for a war. Dried roots, bundled herbs, wax-sealed pastes, lint, thread, needles, a small iron case of knives. A pile of rolled blankets in one corner. A heap of wooden splints. She has made lists, and the lists have made lists.

"You cannot possibly carry all that," says Tian Mo.

"I can carry what I need." She does not look up. "I am going into a country I know nothing about to wake seven children who have been asleep for six hundred years. I would like to have bandages."

"They may not be hurt."

"They may be anything." She pauses with a jar in her hand. "Master Tian. I want to ask you something and I want you to answer without being kind."

"I will try."

"Will it hold?" She turns. Her eyes are Qinghe's, sharp and dark and a little frightened. "The Garden. While we are gone. I am the clinic. I know what is coming in the winters, the fevers, the broken arms. I do not know what is coming from the north. Ning will not tell me. Feng will not tell me. They have the same look, the two of them, as people who have heard a rumor of the sea."

He is silent. Then, because she asked him not to be kind, he tells her.

"I do not know. I think something is coming. I think it is large. I think the Wall that has stood for six hundred years may not hold this season." He meets her eyes. "I will stand on the stair. Whatever comes, it will have to come through me. But I cannot hold the Wall."

She nods slowly. She does not weep. She lays the jar down in the crate with great care and sets her palms on the edge.

"Thank you," she says. "That was not kind."

"No."

"It was exactly right." She straightens, wipes her hands on her apron, and hands him a small linen pouch. "Willow bark and cloves. For the toothache. You've had it for three days and you think nobody has noticed."

He takes it. He finds that he is smiling.

* * *

On the eighth evening, Qinghe does something she has not done in fifty years: she loses her temper at supper.

It is a full table. The family has assembled in the kitchen, as it always does, forty or fifty of them on benches and stools and the edge of the hearth, and the air is thick with steam and the smell of ginger and the sounds of children. She is at the stove, ladling soup. Jian is at the end of the table with Lin Kuang beside him, a lanky solemn boy of thirteen with a face like a small owl, and Yue is next to him, signing, and Bell is arguing with a cousin about the proper dose of willow bark. It is an ordinary scene. It looks like every other night of his life.

"I am coming with you," says Qinghe.

The soup ladle clangs against the pot. The kitchen goes quiet.

"Mother—"

"I am coming. I have thought about it for three weeks and I have decided." She turns, with a spoon in her hand and her chin up. "I am a hundred and five. I am Foundation. I can walk as far as you can. I have not been farther than the river since the war, and I should like very much to see the sixth door."

"You cannot."

"Why not?"

"Because Father is asleep." He says it gently. "He sleeps until the thaw. If you go, there is no one who knows what to do if he wakes."

"Zhao knows."

"Zhao has three children and a clan."

"Then Bell."

"Bell is coming with me." He lifts his hands, helplessly. "Mother, listen. I am going to the first world. I do not know what is there. I do not know if I will come back. I need to know that the Garden is held by someone who loves it and cannot be argued out of it. There is one person in the world who fits that description."

She stares at him.

"You are not going to say it."

"I am."

"No."

"You hold the Garden." The word is very soft. "You hold Father. You hold the soup. I cannot leave without you holding it."

For a long moment nothing happens. Qinghe's mouth is a white line. Then the spoon in her hand, a long-handled ladle of black iron, comes down on the edge of the table with a crash that makes every cup jump.

"I hate it when you are right," she says.

"I know."

"It is a very unattractive quality."

"I know, Mother."

"Come here." She crosses the kitchen in four steps and seizes his face in both her hands, small, rough and trembling. "You will come back. You will bring all of them. And you will eat three bowls of my soup before you tell me one word about what you saw."

"I will."

"And you." She turns her fierce wet eyes on the shape in his head, the small clear presence in the room. "Little one. You look after him."

I will, says the boy, through Jian's mouth, high and shaky and completely certain.

* * *

Late that night, after everyone has gone to bed, Tian Mo finds the Keeper alone on the stair.

He is sitting on the fifth landing, where Kuang died, with his back against the wall and a blanket over his knees. The lamps have been turned down. His hair is silver in the dimness. He does not look up.

"I thought I would find you here," he says.

"I stand here."

"I know. I wanted to sit where you stand. It's a different thing." He gestures, and Tian lowers himself onto the step beside him, with the staff across his knees. For a time neither of them speaks.

"I can't promise you it won't be hard," Jian says at last. "I wanted to say that. I wanted to say it before I go."

"I know."

"I'll have the road. I'll have my sister and the stone and a doctor. You will have nothing but your stance and a lot of people who think you are Kuang." His voice is quiet. "That is unfair. I am sorry."

"I am not Kuang."

"No."

"I'll be a worse wall."

"Perhaps." There is a pause. "I don't think so. I think you'll be a different one. Kuang held because he could not imagine not holding. You hold because you've decided to." He turns his head. "That is better. It lasts longer."

Tian Mo looks down at his hands. They are large and scarred and steady. He thinks of the blanket, the staff too tall, the cold stair at dawn.

"What if I fail?"

"Then you'll fail standing." Jian's mouth curves, a little. "And someone will pick up your staff. That's all a wall is, Tian. It's not one man. It's the next man, and the next. It's whoever's there."

The lamps flicker. Far below, in the dark of the Dock, the Gate wall gives off a faint cold sigh.

"Warden of the Stair," says Tian Mo, slowly. "I would like to take the oath."

"Now?"

"Now."

So they do it there, on the cold step where a man died, with no witnesses but a stone creature that has slipped out of the dark and sits at the foot of the stair with his black eyes shining. Jian recites the words. Tian Mo says them back. They are old and short and plain, the oath of the Founders' first gate-keeper, and when he has finished he finds that his hands are shaking, and that the Keeper is smiling, and that it is, to his great surprise, the happiest he has been in years.

"It is done," says Jian. "Thank you."

"Keeper."

"Yes?"

"Come back."

"I will try."

"That is not an answer," says Tian Mo, quietly.

Jian laughs, a short surprised sound. "No," he says. "It is not. You have been listening to my mother."

"Everyone has."

He rises, and offers a hand, and Tian takes it, and pulls him to his feet. In the blue light of the stair they stand for a moment, the old white-haired man and the tall silent one. Then Jian nods, and turns, and begins to climb. Tian Mo watches him go until the dark takes him.

He plants his staff on the fifth landing, and bends his knees, and stands.
